response.observation: Q wins against D on fit macro-F1 in all three positive-class support groups and loses in all three on assessment. Q also makes 301 forced-positive ranking errors to D’s 236, so the deficit extends to choosing among positive relations. These observations leave the cause open.
response.problem: Does D’s learned token weighting transfer better even when the signed token utilities and biases come from Q? The separately trained Q and D scores leave this question unresolved. Its answer bears directly on whether to design another relation measurement.
response.mechanism: I have no task-linked quantum mechanism with a discriminating advantage over a fair classical replacement. The one test I suggest is to substitute D’s normalized attention into the fitted Q checkpoint. This directly intervenes on which tokens supply evidence for each relation.
response.exact_math: For relation r and valid token i, let uᵠᵣᵢ = Cᵠvᵠ(hᵢ) be Q’s scalar token utility and aᴹᵣᵢ the native normalized attention from model M, including its EPS. Replay z*ᵣ = bᵠᵣ + Σᵢ aᴰᵣᵢuᵠᵣᵢ. The exact logit change is δᵣ = Σᵢ(aᴰᵣᵢ − aᵠᵣᵢ)uᵠᵣᵢ. This follows from the supplied affine decoder and assumes aligned tokens, masks and relation IDs. Only the forward weights change. There is no gradient update or theorem claim.
response.distinguishing_prediction: If D’s weighting itself carries a transferable assessment advantage on Q’s utilities, the replay will exceed Q’s 0.389301 assessment all-40 macro-F1. For a true relation t and rival s, the replay reverses a strict Q loss exactly when δₜ − δₛ > zᵠₛ − zᵠₜ. Even very different attentions give δᵣ = 0 when the tokens exchanging mass have equal Q utility.
response.nearest_collision: This is a standard component substitution. Its purpose is to test the learned attention at the point where it changes class margins. It supplies no theoretical novelty.
response.fair_control: Use native Q as the paired control. Each example then has identical inputs, Q utilities and Q biases in both passes. Native D at 0.472501 provides a reference for the size of the observed gap. The substitution includes D’s learned keys and queries through their output weights, so it cannot attribute a gain specifically to dephasing.
response.screen: One inference-only replay on the existing seed-13, 4096-example assessment split using the checkpoints fitted on 8192 examples for 1024 updates. Primary outcome is all-40 macro-F1. Forced-positive errors are descriptive. No new training arms.
response.stop_rule: A replay at or below native Q falsifies the stated directional prediction on this split. A gain establishes that substituting D’s weights is sufficient to improve this checkpoint on these examples. Neither outcome warrants full-scale advancement.
response.limitations: A failed substitution leaves open co-adaptation between D’s attention and its own utilities. A successful substitution still leaves the origin of D’s better weights unresolved. The reused development split supplies no independent confirmation or evidence of an advantage over Gcov.
